title: Nephilim, Anakim and Rephaim
bigQuestion: Why does the Bible keep track of tall clans from Numbers all the way to 1 Samuel, and how have readers explained them?

story.title: Five Smooth Stones in the Valley of Elah
story.kicker: A shepherd boy picks up five stones, and careful readers ask why the story says where his opponent came from.
paragraphs: The Valley of Elah is a wide, shallow valley in the low hills southwest of Jerusalem. In the story told in 1 Samuel 17, two armies camp on the slopes on either side. The Philistines hold one hill. King Saul and the army of Israel hold the other. Between them runs a dry stream bed, lined with smooth stones.

Each day a champion walks out from the Philistine camp. The text names him Goliath of Gath. He wears a bronze helmet and heavy armor. His spear has a head of iron. He calls across the valley for one man to come and fight him alone. Saul's soldiers hear him and stay where they are.

David is the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem. He has come only to bring food to his older brothers. He hears the challenge and offers to go. Saul gives him armor, but David takes it off, because he is not used to it. He goes down to the stream bed and chooses five smooth stones. He puts them in his shepherd's bag and takes his sling.

The story says David speaks of trusting God, not sword or spear. He runs toward the battle line and slings one stone. It strikes Goliath on the forehead, and the champion falls. The Philistine army turns and runs. For thousands of years, readers have told this story as the small one facing the great one.

Careful readers notice one more detail. Goliath came from Gath. Years earlier, the book of Joshua says, a few of the tall Anakim were left in just three cities, and Gath was one of them. Readers have long asked whether that was chance, or a thread the Bible ties through its stories of giants.
story.think: Why might a writer mention where Goliath came from? What can a place name add to a story?

lessons.title: Twelve Scouts in Canaan
lessons.mainIdea: In Numbers 13, Moses sends twelve scouts into Canaan, and they come back with fruit and with fear.
reading: Numbers 13 tells how Moses sent twelve men to scout the land of Canaan. There was one leader from each of the twelve tribes of Israel. Their job was to look at the land, its towns and its people, and then report back. The text says the trip took forty days. In the valley of Eshcol they cut a cluster of grapes so large that two men carried it on a pole.

The scouts passed through *Hebron*, a town in the southern hill country. There they saw three men named Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai. Numbers 13:22 calls them children of Anak. The *Anakim* were a people the Bible remembers as very tall. Their name simply means the descendants of Anak.

When the scouts came back, they agreed the land was rich. But most of them said the towns had walls and the people were too strong. Caleb disagreed. He said Israel could go up and take the land. The rest of the story becomes an argument about what the scouts saw and what it meant.

words.d: a people the Bible describes as very tall, named as descendants of a man called Anak
an ancient town in the southern hill country of Canaan, where the scouts saw the sons of Anak
the old name for the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea

look.title: The Scouting Trip in Numbers 13
rows: Scouts who gave a hopeful report
Men who carried the grape cluster
look.prompt: Only two scouts gave a hopeful report. Numbers 14:6 names them. Who were they, and how many scouts disagreed with them?

check.q: How many scouts did Moses send in Numbers 13?
choices: Three, one for each son of Anak
check.why: Numbers 13 says one leader from each of the twelve tribes went. Forty is the number of days, not scouts.

check.q: In which town did the scouts see Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai?
check.why: Numbers 13:22 says the scouts came to Hebron, where these three children of Anak lived.

check.q: What did Caleb say after the trip?
choices: That the scouts should stay forty more days
That the people of the land were too strong to face
That Israel could go up and take the land
That the grapes were too heavy to bring home
check.why: Caleb disagreed with the fearful scouts. He said Israel was able to go up and take the land (Numbers 13:30).

lessons.title: Grasshoppers and Nephilim
lessons.mainIdea: Numbers 13:33 says the sons of Anak came from the Nephilim, the same rare word used in Genesis 6:4.
reading: The scouts' report ends with a striking line. In Numbers 13:33 they say they saw the *Nephilim* there, and that the sons of Anak came from the Nephilim. Then they add that they felt like grasshoppers, and that is how they looked to those people too. The picture is of small insects looking up at very tall people.

The word Nephilim is rare. It appears in only two places in the Hebrew Bible: here and in Genesis 6:4. In Genesis 6 the Nephilim are on the earth when the sons of God take human wives. The King James Version of 1611 translated the word as giants in both places. The *Septuagint*, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, had already used the Greek word gigantes, giants, in both verses.

So the translators of the Septuagint read the two verses together. Many modern scholars do too. Michael Heiser, in The Unseen Realm (2015), read Numbers 13:33 as a deliberate link to the Genesis 6 story. He also argued that the word Nephilim is best explained from an *Aramaic* word for giants, not from the Hebrew verb for falling. Other scholars prefer the falling root, or leave the question open.

That raises a puzzle. If Nephilim lived before the flood, how could any be around in Moses' day? Genesis 6:4 says the Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward. Readers answer the puzzle in different ways, and later lessons look at them.

words.d: a rare Hebrew word for a group of very tall people, found only in Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun by Jewish scholars around 250 BCE
a language close to Hebrew, spoken widely in the ancient Near East; parts of Daniel and Ezra are in Aramaic

look.title: The Scouts' Last Words
look.text: And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.
look.cite: Numbers 13:33, King James Version (1611). Where the KJV says giants, the Hebrew says Nephilim.
look.prompt: What does the grasshopper comparison tell you about how the scouts felt? Is it describing size, feeling, or both?

check.q: Which two books of the Hebrew Bible use the word Nephilim?
check.why: Nephilim appears only in Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33.

check.q: In Numbers 13:33, what do the scouts compare themselves to?
check.why: The scouts say they seemed like grasshoppers, both to themselves and to the tall people.

check.q: What Greek word did the Septuagint use for Nephilim in Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33?
check.why: The Septuagint used gigantes, giants, in both verses, the same idea the KJV later followed.

lessons.title: A Bad Report?
lessons.mainIdea: Numbers calls the scouts' report a bad report, so some readers think its giant language grew out of fear.
reading: Numbers 13:32 calls the scouts' words an evil report. Many newer translations say a bad report. The scouts said the land eats up the people who live in it. In chapter 14 the whole camp weeps and talks of going back to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and urge the people not to be afraid.

Because the text itself calls the report bad, some readers doubt the giant line. They think frightened scouts made their enemies sound bigger than they were. On this reading, Nephilim is the scouts' scary label, not the narrator's own description. The book of Numbers, they note, puts these words in the mouths of the fearful ten.

Other readers point elsewhere. Deuteronomy 2 and 9 and Joshua 11 and 15 also speak of the Anakim as very tall, and those words come from the narrator, not from the scouts. On this view, the problem with the report was the scouts' lack of trust, not an invented enemy. Readers still weigh both views, and the text leaves room to discuss each one.

words.d: the phrase Numbers 13:32 uses for the scouts' discouraging account; many translations say bad report
making something sound bigger or worse than it really is
the voice that tells a story, as opposed to the characters who speak inside it

look.title: Two Ways to Hear the Scouts
look.text: Reading A: The scouts really saw very tall people, and they described them truly. Their failure was fear and a lack of trust. Reading B: The scouts were afraid, so they made their enemies sound huge, borrowing an old and scary name from the past.
look.prompt: Find one detail in Numbers 13 and 14 that Reading A could point to, and one that Reading B could point to.

check.q: How does Numbers 13:32 describe the scouts' account?
choices: As a true and faithful report
As an evil or bad report
check.why: Numbers 13:32 calls it an evil report; many newer translations say bad report.

check.q: Which two scouts urged the people not to be afraid?
check.why: Numbers 14:6-9 says Joshua and Caleb tore their clothes and told the people not to fear.

check.q: Why do some readers think the Nephilim line was exaggeration?
choices: Numbers never mentions the Anakim at all
Caleb is the one who spoke the line
The scouts said the land had no people
The text calls the report bad, and the words come from frightened scouts
check.why: The narrator calls the report bad, and the Nephilim line is spoken by the ten fearful scouts.

lessons.title: Emim and Zamzummim
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 2 says nearby nations had their own names for tall peoples, and it groups them all as Rephaim.
reading: Deuteronomy 2 pauses its travel story to give a short history lesson. As Israel passes Moab, the text says a people called the *Emim* once lived there. They were great, many and tall like the Anakim. The Moabites called them Emim. But the text says they were also counted among the *Rephaim* (Deuteronomy 2:10-11).

A few verses later, the same thing happens in the land of Ammon. Deuteronomy 2:20-21 says the Ammonites called the old tall people there *Zamzummim*. They too were counted as Rephaim. The text says God destroyed them before the Ammonites, who then settled in their place.

So one kind of people had several names. Anakim, Emim and Zamzummim were local names, and Rephaim was the wider label. Deuteronomy explains this almost like a note on a map. Many scholars think these notes were added by a later editor to explain old names to readers. Either way, the text tracks tall clans on both sides of the Jordan.

words.d: a Hebrew word used for tall clans in Deuteronomy and Joshua, and for the dead in other books
the Moabite name for a tall people who lived in Moab before them (Deuteronomy 2:10-11)
the Ammonite name for a tall people who lived in Ammon before them (Deuteronomy 2:20-21)

look.title: A Map With Notes
look.text: Picture a map east of the Jordan River. In Moab, a small note reads: Emim, the Moabite name, also called Rephaim. Farther north, in Ammon, another note reads: Zamzummim, the Ammonite name, also called Rephaim. West of the Jordan, around Hebron: Anakim, also counted as Rephaim.
look.prompt: Why might a writer stop a travel story to explain local names? What does it tell you about the readers the writer had in mind?

check.q: What did the Moabites call the tall people who lived in Moab before them?
check.why: Deuteronomy 2:11 says the Moabites called them Emim.

check.q: In Deuteronomy 2, what wider name covers the Emim, Zamzummim and Anakim?
check.why: Deuteronomy 2:11 and 2:20 count these peoples as Rephaim.

check.q: According to Deuteronomy 2:20-21, who settled where the Zamzummim had lived?
check.why: The Zamzummim lived in the land the Ammonites later settled; the Edomites settled Seir, a different place.

lessons.title: Og and His Iron Bed
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 3:11 calls Og of Bashan the last of the Rephaim and describes his huge iron bed.
reading: *Og* was king of Bashan, a region east of the Jordan River. Numbers 21 and Deuteronomy 3 tell how Israel fought his army at Edrei and won. Then Deuteronomy 3:11 adds a note. It says Og alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim. The text treats him as the last of an old line.

The same verse describes his bed, or bedstead, made of iron. It was nine cubits long and four cubits wide. A *cubit* was a measure from the elbow to the fingertip, about 18 inches. So the bed was about 13 and a half feet long and 6 feet wide. The verse says it could still be seen in Rabbah of the Ammonites. That city is Amman, in Jordan, today.

Readers explain the bed in different ways. Some take the verse as a plain record of a very tall king. Some scholars suggest the bed was a ceremonial couch, sized for display rather than sleep. Some older commentators thought the word for iron might describe dark basalt stone. Either way, the verse's main point is that Og belonged to the Rephaim.

words.d: the king of Bashan in Numbers 21 and Deuteronomy 3, called the last of the remnant of the Rephaim
an ancient measure from the elbow to the fingertip, about 18 inches
a fertile region east and northeast of the Sea of Galilee, ruled by Og in the Bible

look.title: How Big Was Og's Bed?
look.cite: Deuteronomy 3:11; feet worked out with a cubit of about 18 inches
look.prompt: A tall adult today is about 6 feet. How many of them could lie end to end along Og's bed?

check.q: What does Deuteronomy 3:11 say about Og?
choices: He was the first of the Nephilim
He alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim
He was a scout sent by Moses
He was the champion of Gath
check.why: Deuteronomy 3:11 says only Og remained of the remnant of the Rephaim.

check.q: About how long was Og's bed, using an 18-inch cubit?
check.why: Nine cubits times 18 inches is 162 inches, about 13 and a half feet. Nine is the number of cubits, not feet.

check.q: Where did Deuteronomy say Og's bed could still be seen?
choices: In Edrei, where Og's army fought
check.why: Deuteronomy 3:11 says the bed was in Rabbah of the Ammonites, today's Amman.

lessons.title: The Anakim Who Remained
lessons.mainIdea: Joshua 11:21-22 says Joshua removed the Anakim from the hill country, but some stayed in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod.
reading: The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered Canaan. Near the end of its war stories, Joshua 11:21 says Joshua cut off the Anakim from the hill country. It names Hebron, Debir and Anab. Later, Joshua 15:14 says Caleb drove out the three sons of Anak from Hebron. They are the same three names the scouts had seen.

Then Joshua 11:22 adds an exception. No Anakim were left in Israel's land, it says, except in Gaza, in *Gath* and in Ashdod. These three cities lay on the coastal plain in the southwest. In later books of the Bible, all three are cities of the *Philistines*.

Many readers see this verse as a setup. It leaves a few of the tall clans in the very places where Israel's later enemies live. When a giant warrior comes out of Gath in 1 Samuel, readers who remember Joshua 11:22 notice. Other readers see the verse as a plain record of places Israel did not take.

words.d: a Philistine city on the coastal plain, named as Goliath's hometown
a people on the southern coast of Canaan, often at war with Israel in the books of Samuel

look.title: Three Cities Left
look.text: There was none of the Anakims left in the land of the children of Israel: only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod, there remained.
look.prompt: Name the three cities in this verse. Which one comes back in the story of David?

check.q: In which three cities does Joshua 11:22 say Anakim remained?
check.why: Joshua 11:22 names Gaza, Gath and Ashdod. Hebron, Debir and Anab are the places they were removed from.

check.q: Who drove the three sons of Anak out of Hebron, according to Joshua 15:14?
check.why: Joshua 15:14 says Caleb drove out Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai, the sons of Anak.

check.q: Why do many readers think Joshua 11:22 matters for the David story?
choices: It leaves Anakim in Gath, Goliath's hometown
It shows the Philistines came from Bashan
It says David was born in Gaza
It names Goliath as one of the scouts
check.why: Joshua 11:22 leaves Anakim in Gath, and Goliath later comes from Gath (1 Samuel 17:4).

lessons.title: A Champion From Gath
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Samuel 17 presents Goliath as a heavily armed Philistine champion from Gath.
reading: 1 Samuel 17 introduces Goliath with care. He is a *champion*, a man who fights one-on-one for his whole army. The Hebrew phrase means, word for word, the man between, the one who stands in the space between two battle lines. He comes from Gath, one of the chief Philistine cities.

The writer lists his gear. He has a bronze helmet and a coat of scale armor weighing five thousand *shekels* of bronze. That is roughly 125 pounds. His spear shaft is like a weaver's beam, and its iron point alone weighs six hundred shekels. The long list is on purpose. It makes the reader feel how outmatched Saul's army seemed.

David's answer turns the scene. In 1 Samuel 17:45 he says, in effect, that Goliath comes with sword and spear, but he comes in the name of the LORD. Jewish and Christian readers have long read the story as trust set against might. The hometown adds another layer: Goliath of Gath recalls the Anakim left in Gath in Joshua 11:22.

The Gath thread does not end with Goliath. 2 Samuel 21:15-22 tells of four more warriors from Gath. They are called descendants of the Rapha, which the KJV translates as the giant. Many scholars connect that word with the Rephaim. One of the four had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot. David's soldiers defeated all four.

words.d: a warrior who fights one-on-one for a whole army; in Hebrew, the man between the battle lines
an ancient unit of weight, a little over 11 grams, later also the name of a coin
the name 2 Samuel 21 gives as the ancestor of four warriors from Gath; the KJV says the giant

look.title: Goliath Steps Out
look.text: And there went out a champion out of the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath, of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span.
look.prompt: This verse gives Goliath's hometown and his height. The next lesson compares the height in different old manuscripts. What do you predict you will find?

check.q: What was a champion in 1 Samuel 17?
choices: A priest who blessed the soldiers
A warrior who fought one-on-one for his whole army
A king who ruled a Philistine city
A scout who spied on the enemy
check.why: Goliath is a champion, literally the man between the battle lines, who fights for his side alone.

check.q: According to 2 Samuel 21:20, what was unusual about one warrior from Gath?
choices: He slept on an iron bed nine cubits long
He came from the land of Bashan
He had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot
check.why: 2 Samuel 21:20 describes a warrior of Gath with six fingers and six toes; the iron bed belongs to Og.

check.q: What does 1 Samuel 17:45 say David comes with?
check.why: In 1 Samuel 17:45 David says Goliath comes with sword and spear, but he comes in the name of the LORD.

lessons.title: Two Heights for Goliath
lessons.mainIdea: Old manuscripts disagree on Goliath's height: about nine feet nine inches in one, about six feet nine inches in others.
reading: Most English Bibles translate the *Masoretic Text*, the standard Hebrew text. Jewish scribes called Masoretes copied it with great care. Its oldest complete copy is the Leningrad Codex, from about 1008 CE. In 1 Samuel 17:4 it says Goliath was six cubits and a *span* tall. A span is about half a cubit. That makes about nine feet nine inches.

Other old witnesses read differently. A Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel from Qumran Cave 4, called 4QSamuel-a, was copied around 50 BCE. It reads four cubits and a span. Most copies of the Greek Septuagint also read four. So does the Jewish historian Josephus, writing around 94 CE. Four cubits and a span is about six feet nine inches.

Which reading is older? Scholars who practice *textual criticism*, the careful comparing of manuscripts, disagree. Some think a copyist raised the number over time. Others defend the Masoretic reading. Either way, a man about six feet nine inches tall, in full armor, would have stood far above most soldiers of his day.

words.d: the standard Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, carefully copied by Jewish scribes called Masoretes
an ancient measure from the thumb to the little finger of a spread hand, about half a cubit
the careful comparing of manuscripts to learn how a text was copied and which reading is oldest

look.title: Goliath's Height in Four Witnesses
rows: Masoretic Text: 6 cubits and a span
Dead Sea Scroll 4QSamuel-a: 4 cubits and a span
Septuagint, most copies: 4 cubits and a span
Josephus, Antiquities: 4 cubits and a span
look.cite: 1 Samuel 17:4 in each witness; feet worked out with an 18-inch cubit and a 9-inch span
look.prompt: How many witnesses read four cubits? Does counting witnesses settle which reading is oldest? Why or why not?

check.q: What height does the Masoretic Text give Goliath?
check.why: The Masoretic Text of 1 Samuel 17:4 reads six cubits and a span, about nine feet nine inches.

check.q: Which old sources read four cubits and a span?
choices: A Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel and most Septuagint copies
The Leningrad Codex and the King James Version
check.why: 4QSamuel-a and most Septuagint copies read four. The Leningrad Codex and the KJV follow the Masoretic six.

check.q: What is textual criticism?
choices: Comparing manuscripts to learn how a text was copied
Writing new endings to old stories
Deciding whether a story is true or false
check.why: Textual criticism compares manuscripts, like 4QSamuel-a and the Masoretic Text, to trace how a text was copied.

lessons.title: A Thread From Genesis 6
lessons.mainIdea: Ancient and modern readers have tied the giant clans of Canaan back to the Nephilim of Genesis 6.
reading: Put the verses side by side. Genesis 6:4 names the Nephilim. Numbers 13:33 says the sons of Anak came from the Nephilim. Deuteronomy 2 and 3 count the Anakim and others as Rephaim. Joshua 11:22 leaves Anakim in Gath. 1 Samuel 17 sends out a champion from Gath. Read in order, the verses form a chain.

Ancient Jewish writers already connected giants with Genesis 6. 1 Enoch 7 says the *sons of God*, whom it calls Watchers, fathered great giants. Fragments of a Book of Giants, found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, tell more of their story. Loren Stuckenbruck studied those fragments in The Book of Giants from Qumran (1997). Josephus, writing around 94 CE, compared the children of angels in Genesis 6 to the giants of Greek stories.

Michael Heiser, in The Unseen Realm (2015), argued that the biblical writers wove this chain on purpose. He read each of the sons of God as a *divine being* who crossed a line, and the giant clans as the lasting *fallout* of that rebellion. That, he argued, is why the conquest stories pay the clans so much attention.

What about the flood? If the Nephilim died in the flood, how could they appear later? Genesis 6:4 says the Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward. Readers have offered several answers, such as the same kind of event happening again after the flood. The text itself does not say how.

words.d: the figures in Genesis 6:2-4 who take human wives; read by some as divine beings, by others as human men
a being of the heavenly world, such as an angel or a member of God's heavenly council
the lasting results of an event, especially a bad one

look.title: Josephus on Genesis 6
look.text: Josephus says that many angels of God joined with women and had sons who were unjust and proud of their strength. He adds that their deeds were like those the Greeks told about their giants.
look.cite: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 1.3.1, trans. William Whiston (1737); paraphrased
look.prompt: Josephus compares Genesis 6 to Greek stories his readers knew. Why might a writer explain a Jewish text that way?

check.q: Which phrase in Genesis 6:4 helps readers explain giants after the flood?
check.why: Genesis 6:4 says the Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward.

check.q: Which ancient book says the Watchers fathered great giants?
check.why: 1 Enoch 7 retells Genesis 6 and says the Watchers' children were great giants.

check.q: In Heiser's reading, what did the giant clans stand for?
choices: The lasting fallout of the rebellion in Genesis 6
check.why: In The Unseen Realm (2015), Heiser tied the clans to the sons of God in Genesis 6.

lessons.title: Other Ways to Read the Giants
lessons.mainIdea: Many readers see the giant clans as tall warriors, or as enemies made larger in ancient war writing.
reading: Not every reader sees a thread from Genesis 6. One common view is that the Anakim and Rephaim were simply tall peoples. Tall families and tall warriors appear in every age. On this reading, the Bible remembers real enemies who stood out, with no link to heavenly beings.

A second view looks at how ancient people wrote about war. Kings and scribes across the ancient Near East often made enemies sound huge and victories total. Some scholars read the giant language as this kind of *hyperbole*. It shows, they say, that Israel's God gave victory against impossible odds. The scouts' bad report in Numbers 13 fits this reading too.

A third group reads the sons of God in Genesis 6 as human. Early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr read them as angels. Later, Julius Africanus and Augustine favored men from the family line of Seth, the *Sethite view*. Many Jewish readers took them to be powerful rulers. Annette Yoshiko Reed, in Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity (2005), traces how these readings rose and fell.

Some modern books claim that giants built the pyramids or came from other planets. Scholars of the Bible, whatever their reading, reject such claims. A good check is simple: open the text and see whether it actually says so. None of these verses mention pyramids or other worlds.

words.d: deliberate exaggeration used for effect, common in ancient war writing
the reading that the sons of God in Genesis 6 were men from the family line of Seth

look.title: Three Readings, One Verse
look.text: Take Numbers 13:33. Thread reading: the writer links the Anakim to the Nephilim of Genesis 6 on purpose. Tall-warrior reading: the Anakim were very tall people, and the scouts named them with an old word. Hyperbole reading: frightened scouts, and later writers, made the enemy sound larger than life.
look.prompt: Pick a different verse from this chapter. How would each of the three readings explain it?

check.q: What is the Sethite view of Genesis 6?
choices: Seth was the first of the Nephilim
The sons of God were men from the family line of Seth
The sons of God were giants from Bashan
The sons of God were Philistine kings
check.why: The Sethite view reads the sons of God as human men descended from Seth.

check.q: Why do some scholars think the giant language is hyperbole?
choices: The Hebrew word for giant means grasshopper
Giants appear only in the Septuagint
Ancient war writing often made enemies sound huge
check.why: Across the ancient Near East, war reports often enlarged enemies and victories.

check.q: Which early Christian writer favored the Sethite view?
check.why: Augustine, like Julius Africanus before him, read the sons of God as men from Seth's line; Justin Martyr read them as angels.

lessons.title: Rephaim: Giants and the Dead
lessons.mainIdea: The word Rephaim names giant clans in some verses and the spirits of the dead in others.
reading: Rephaim is a puzzling word. In Deuteronomy and Joshua it names tall clans. In other books it names the dead. Psalm 88:10 asks whether the Rephaim will rise and praise God, and the King James Version translates the word as the dead. Isaiah 14:9, Isaiah 26:14 and Proverbs 9:18 use it the same way, for those in the realm of the dead.

Clay tablets from *Ugarit* help explain this. Ugarit was an ancient city on the coast of Syria. It was destroyed around 1185 BCE, and its tablets were found from 1929 on. Its texts speak of the rpum, a word scholars connect with Rephaim. In these texts they are honored ancestors, especially dead kings, remembered in ceremonies for the royal family.

Heiser argued the two uses belong together. In his reading, the biblical writers linked the giant clans with the shadowy dead of the *underworld*, and the one word carried both ideas. Many other scholars think the word simply had two meanings. Some suggest that old warrior kings came to be remembered as the mighty dead. Either way, knowing both uses helps readers of Isaiah and the Psalms.

words.d: an ancient city on the Syrian coast whose clay tablets, found from 1929 on, shed light on the Hebrew Bible
the realm of the dead; in the Hebrew Bible it is often called Sheol
a word in the tablets of Ugarit for honored dead ancestors, connected by scholars with Rephaim

look.title: A Question in the Psalms
look.text: Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee? Selah.
look.cite: Psalm 88:10, King James Version (1611). The Hebrew word translated the dead is rephaim.
look.prompt: The same Hebrew word names Og's clan in Deuteronomy. What changes when you read it here as the dead?

check.q: How does the KJV translate rephaim in Psalm 88:10?
check.why: In Psalm 88:10 the KJV renders rephaim as the dead.

check.q: Where was Ugarit?
check.why: Ugarit was a city on the Syrian coast; its tablets were found from 1929 on.

check.q: What did Heiser argue about the two uses of Rephaim?
choices: They are two unrelated words that only look alike
They were both invented by the Septuagint
They belong together, linking giant clans and the dead
check.why: Heiser read the giant clans and the dead Rephaim as linked ideas carried by one word.

review.q: Which verse says the sons of Anak came from the Nephilim?
review.why: Numbers 13:33 is the scouts' line linking the sons of Anak to the Nephilim.

review.q: What is Og called in Deuteronomy 3:11?
choices: A scout who returned with grapes
The last of the remnant of the Rephaim
review.why: Deuteronomy 3:11 says Og alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim.

review.q: The Emim and Zamzummim were local names for which wider group?
review.why: Deuteronomy 2:11 and 2:20 count both peoples as Rephaim.

review.q: How do manuscripts differ on Goliath's height?
choices: The Masoretic Text says six cubits and a span; a Dead Sea Scroll says four
All manuscripts agree he was nine cubits
Only the King James Version gives a height
review.why: The Masoretic Text reads six cubits and a span, while 4QSamuel-a and most Septuagint copies read four.

review.q: Which verse leaves Anakim in Gath, Goliath's hometown?
review.why: Joshua 11:22 leaves Anakim in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod, and Goliath comes from Gath.

review.q: Which is a reading of the giant stories that does not see a thread from Genesis 6?
choices: They describe tall warriors, enlarged by ancient war writing
They describe the kings of Ugarit
They describe the twelve scouts' families
They describe the Masoretes who copied the text
review.why: Many readers see the clans as tall peoples, described with the hyperbole common in ancient war reports.

review.q: Besides giant clans, what else can Rephaim mean in the Hebrew Bible?
review.why: In Psalm 88:10, Isaiah 26:14 and Proverbs 9:18, rephaim means the dead.

review.q: Which ancient city's tablets speak of the rpum?
review.why: The tablets of Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, speak of the rpum as honored dead ancestors.
